children: 〔生物多样性评估作为一项多元文化的实践〕

Knowledge grows through multiple layers of collaboration—as both empathy and betrayal. The process of layering is perhaps most striking in insignificant, vernacular collaborations—like the one I catalyzed in the village of Kalawan, at a moment when a much-cherished biodiversity was becoming an issue of anxious concern.
知识通过层层叠叠的协作而生长——其中既有共情，也有背叛。分层的过程或许在最不起眼的地方性协作中最为醒目，就像我在卡拉万村促成的那一次；当时，一种备受珍视的生物多样性正成为一个令人焦虑的问题。

1994. It started with an innocent question about eels; I was thinking of dinner. “Are there any eels in the river?” I asked. Uma Adang, my Meratus Dayak friend and mentor, leaned back, assuming her most serious oratorical bearing. “Facing the year 2000,” she proclaimed, “we must make a list of all the contents of this earth, this island Borneo.” Plants and animals, their names and uses and local or foreign locations: all, she told me, should be listed. I was taken aback. I had not yet had the chance to explain much to her about my new research on global environmentalism. She was not in touch with global biodiversity experts, although surely some radio announcer or nature hiker had brought the rhetoric of environmentalism to her village. Yet she beautifully articulated the spirit of environmental prophecy: the looming, apocalyptic crisis of nature as revealed at the turn of the millennium, the chance to save the earth through proper naming, and the necessity, in doing so, of moving back and forth between “the island” and “the earth”—the minutely local and the whole globe.

1994年。事情始于一个关于鳗鱼的天真问题；我当时在琢磨晚饭。“河里有鳗鱼吗？”我问。我的梅拉图斯达雅克朋友兼导师乌玛·阿当向后靠了靠，摆出她最严肃的演讲姿态。“面对2000年，”她宣称，“我们必须制作一份名录，列出这大地、这婆罗洲岛的全部内容。”植物和动物，它们的名称、用途，以及本地或外地的位置：她说，所有这些都应列入。我吃了一惊。我还没来得及多向她解释我关于全球环保主义的新研究。她并未接触过全球生物多样性专家，尽管肯定有某个电台播音员或自然徒步者把环保主义的话语带到了她的村子。然而，她出色地表达了环境预言的精神：千禧年之交显现的、迫近的自然末日危机；通过正确命名来拯救大地的机会；以及在此过程中，必须在“岛屿”与“大地”之间——在极其本地之物与整个地球之间——来回移动的必要性。

Over the next ten days, Uma Adang sat with me and dictated over a thousand local life-forms. She wasn’t feeling well, and she didn’t want to go outside. Instead, she felt happier sitting with me on the floor of her house, telling me about plants and animals. Every now and again, someone else in the household, feeling the pleasure of our work, would come in with a plant sample picked outside: “You haven’t listed this yet.” We would add a new name to our list. Or, restless, I would follow someone to gather river snails or fern fiddleheads for dinner, and another name would emerge. But most of the time we were deprived of the stimulus of the plants and animals around us and left, instead, with Uma Adang’s memory and imagination. Nor had we books of flora and fauna to recall more species to mind; we had to remember an organism to place it on the list, and, in the context of this oral recitation, we almost never went back to add forgotten species to earlier categories. We missed a good many plants and animals we both knew—and, I’m sure, many more with which I am unfamiliar. Still, more than one thousand life-forms is not bad. I have been told that U.S. Americans, asked to do a similar task and with less local specificity, could not list more than several hundred. Uma Adang self-consciously limited herself to living things that were found in her local area, a karst-studded plain of small shifting fields and still-large but threatened forests at the foot of the Meratus Mountains. She excluded life-forms that she knew occurred at the coast, as that, she said, should be a different list. This was a self-conscious project of placing a local niche within a global imagining. The lists acknowledged and acclaimed global biodiversity by conserving a local space within it.

接下来的十天里，乌玛·阿当坐在我身边，口述了一千多种本地生命形式。她身体不适，不想出门。她反倒更愿意和我坐在她家的地板上，给我讲植物和动物。时不时地，家里另一个人感受到我们这项工作的乐趣，会拿着从外面采来的植物样本走进来：“这个你还没列进去。”我们便往名录里增添一个新名字。或者，我坐不住，就跟着某人去捡河螺或采蕨菜芽当晚饭，于是又有一个名字浮现出来。但大多数时候，我们无法受到身边植物和动物的刺激，只能依靠乌玛·阿当的记忆和想象。我们也没有植物志和动物志可供回想更多物种；我们必须先记起一种生物，才能把它列入名录，而在这种口头背诵的情境中，我们几乎从不回头把遗忘的物种补进先前的类别。我们漏掉了许多彼此都认识的植物和动物——而且我确信，还有更多我不认识的。不过，一千多种生命形式也不错了。我听说，让美国人做类似的事，且本地特异性更少，他们最多只能列出几百种。乌玛·阿当有意识地限定在本地能找到的生物：梅拉图斯山脚下点缀着喀斯特地貌的平原，上面散布着小块刀耕火种田，以及面积仍然可观却受到威胁的森林。她排除了她所知道生长在海岸的生命形式，因为她说，那应当是另一份名录。这是一个有意识的工程：把本地的小生境放进全球想象之中。这些名录承认并赞美全球生物多样性，方式是在其中保全一个本地空间。

Because I had asked about eels, we began with laba’ di ai’ing, beings of the water. Uma Adang listed the best fish to eat, and then some less significant fish, then the fish found in swamps, the reptiles, the amphibians, the mollusks, the crustaceans, and finally the water plants. Because I had watched people fish and admired their catch, the list easily evoked the everyday livelihood practices through which I, too, could call to mind these water creatures. Wading in deep river pools, young men threw hand-woven nets to catch the sweet-fleshed iwak. In the mountains, men bent bamboo poles, their ends craftily hooked underwater so that they sprung straight up when a fish took the bait, leaving the iwak swinging high over the river. When the iwak were big, people divided them up in small chunks, counting out equal shares for every household just as if they were game. In Uma Adang’s network, boys swam underwater with home-made goggles and rubber-band-powered spear-guns to bring us delicious kambalang and lampam. Woven bamboo traps caught smaller fish in fast-running streams. In muddy creek holes, we could build a tiny dam and scoop up saluwang minnows with our hands; we steamed and ate them, bones and all. I myself once brought home a great panting catfish; it had been killed by a bird, which flew away when I ran up, leaving its fresh prey. As for turtles, frogs, shrimp, and snails: We had enjoyed them all. And, of course, eels.

The taste of food was not, however, the only pleasure called up in this list. Uma Adang is alert to the colors, textures, and sounds of the beings around her. She described the karantung frog as “the music of the deep water” and mimicked its call. She knows plants and animals in relation to locations: She tried to remind me of the place I had just seen the water plant tantamau, on the rocks where we were gathering snails. Sometimes forest birds and animals become companions: I saw my first kuntan tortoise when I was introduced to Uma Adang’s latest pet, whom she brought home from the forest to coax and protect and feed ripe bananas as it crawled around the house. As for riverside lua’ trees, we talked as much about the animals attracted to the tree because of its fruit as about its human uses.
然而，食物的滋味并不是这份名录唤起的唯一乐趣。乌玛·阿当对周围生灵的颜色、质地和声音十分敏感。她把
蛙描述为“深水之乐”，并模仿它的叫声。她认识植物和动物时，总是联系着地点：她试图提醒我，我刚刚在捡螺的岩石上见过水生植物
。有时森林鸟类和动物会成为伴侣：我第一次见到
龟，是有人介绍我认识乌玛·阿当最新的宠物时；她从森林里把它带回家，哄着它、保护它，当它在屋里爬来爬去时喂它熟香蕉。至于河岸的
树，我们谈论被果实吸引到树上的动物，和谈论它对人的用途一样多。

Meanwhile, the river was becoming a difficult place to find food. With the building of new roads, the practice of sending an electric current into the water with a car battery had been introduced to Uma Adang’s area. All the fish, big and small, died. (At least one person died too, by accidentally slipping into the water while the electric current was still active.) The rivers were becoming barren. Uma Adang’s worries about this situation provoked her attention to listing the river’s denizens. Her list was a form of apology that soon enough we would not be eating and even encountering these fish and frogs and eels. A prospective, incipient nostalgia helped motivate the list: the same incipient nostalgia as that which motivates so much of the science of environmental conservation, particularly concerning the conservation of biodiversity.

与此同时，河流越来越难以找到食物。随着新道路的修建，有人把一种做法引入了乌玛·阿当所在的地区：用汽车电瓶向水中通电。大鱼小鱼全都死了。（还有至少一个人死去，他不小心在电流仍然开着的时候滑进了水里。）河流正在变得荒芜。乌玛·阿当对这种状况的担忧，促使她关注为河流居民编列名录。她的名录是一种致歉，因为很快我们就不会吃、甚至不会再遇见这些鱼、蛙和鳗了。一种预期性的、初生的怀旧情绪推动了这份名录：那种同样推动着大量环境保护科学——尤其是生物多样性保护——的初生怀旧情绪。

Incipient nostalgia had caught us, enlivening our encounter. Indeed, the globalism of our exercise meant that our list was charged by emotions, quests, and voices originating from many sites, each buffeting us with their whiffs of pleasure, charisma, terror, dead authority, or charm. They crowd around me now, in telling the tale, bringing their eccentric habits and irascible opinions to any purpose we might have concocted.
初生的怀旧情绪攫住了我们，使我们的相遇变得活跃。确实，我们这项实践的全球主义意味着，名录被来自许多场所的情感、追寻和声音所充能；它们各自向我们送来一缕缕快感、感召力、恐惧、僵死的权威或魅力。如今在讲述这个故事时，它们挤在我周围，带着古怪的习惯和暴躁的意见，投入我们可能编造出的任何目的。

The biologist, E. O. Wilson, fresh from communion with ants, rises to proclaim with reverence: “the diversity of life is the cradle and greatest natural heritage of the human species” (Wilson in Takacs 1996: 309).
生物学家 E. O. 威尔逊刚与蚂蚁交流完毕，便带着敬意起身宣告：“生命的多样性是人类物种的摇篮和最伟大的自然遗产”（Wilson in Takacs 1996: 309）。

Since the 1980s, biodiversity has developed as an object of worldwide concern: the centerpiece of global environmentalism. Public awareness of biodiversity draws from the visibility of conservation biology: the science that grows from taking the threat of species extinctions seriously. Conservation biology is self-consciously action-oriented as well as research-driven (Noss and Cooperrider 1994). Crossing lines between science and policy, it asks us to care about the abundance of species in every corner of the earth. Listing species is significant because it allows us to discover variety and to appreciate its dynamics.

自20世纪80年代以来，生物多样性已发展为一个全球关切的对象：全球环保主义的核心。公众对生物多样性的认知，源于保护生物学的可见度：这门科学从认真对待物种灭绝的威胁中成长起来。保护生物学自觉地既以行动为导向，也以研究为驱动（Noss and Cooperrider 1994）。它跨越科学与政策的界线，要求我们关心地球每个角落里物种的丰盛。为物种编列名录之所以重要，是因为它让我们发现多样性，并欣赏其动态。

My mother, the only Chinese American member of an Ohio wild flowers society, tells me: “Learning the names of plants is just like learning the names of people you meet; when you know their names, you can get to know them better.”
我母亲是俄亥俄州一个野花协会里唯一的华裔美国人。她对我说：“学习植物的名字，就像学习你遇见的人的名字；知道了他们的名字，你才能更好地认识他们。”

The idea of biodiversity has proved charismatic because it combines the scientific legitimacy of biology with popular legacies of plant and animal identification. Victorian amateur collectors, particularly in England and its diaspora, were fascinated by the variety of nature (Dunlap 1999). The theory of evolution interpolated species collecting into one of the most thrilling sciences of the times. Similarly, conservation biology energizes contemporary popular practices of nature appreciation in which learning the names of species creates a vitalizing intimacy with nature (Wilson 1992). Species-oriented nature appreciation—from birdwatching to wildlife television— had a well-established place in late twentieth century metropolitan cultures. Conservation biologists were able to draw on this popularity, and build it, as they showed the importance of conserving the diversity of nature. Working together across lay and technical lines, conservation biologists and environmental activists have made attention to biodiversity—including the practice of making species lists—the first requirement of conservation itself.

生物多样性观念被证明有感召力，因为它把生物学的科学正当性与植物和动物鉴定的民间传统结合起来。维多利亚时代的业余采集者，尤其是在英格兰及其海外移民地，迷恋自然的多样性（Dunlap 1999）。进化论把采集物种插入当时最激动人心的科学之一。同样，保护生物学也为当代自然欣赏的流行实践注入活力；在这些实践中，学习物种名称创造出一种使人焕发生机的与自然的亲近（Wilson 1992）。以物种为导向的自然欣赏——从观鸟到野生动物电视——在20世纪晚期的大都会文化中已有牢固位置。保护生物学家能够利用并扩大这种流行性，同时展示保护自然多样性的重要性。保护生物学家和环保行动者跨越业余与专业的界线共同工作，使对生物多样性的关注——包括编制物种名录的实践——成为保护本身的首要要求。

The environmental activists of the Rainforest Action Network transmit the latest communiqué from the U’wa people of Colombia: “We U’wa will not cede our cultural, historic, and ancient rights. We prefer genocide sponsored by the Colombian government rather than handing over our Mother Earth to the oil companies” (Cabildo Mayor U’wa 2000).
雨林行动网络的环保行动者转发了哥伦比亚乌瓦人最新的公告：“我们乌瓦人不会放弃我们的文化、历史和古老权利。我们宁愿死于哥伦比亚政府资助的种族灭绝，也不愿把我们的地球母亲交给石油公司”（Cabildo Mayor U’wa 2000）。

The blossoming of the international campaign to save the Amazon forest in the late 1980s inspired a new political form: collaborations between indigenous leaders and environmentalists. Indigenous rights became entangled with conservation initiatives. Such collaborations were inspired in part by researchers who had found that indigenous people appreciated and managed the biodiversity with which they lived (e.g., Posey 1985). It seemed possible that culturally sensitive alliances among scientists, activists, and indigenous peoples might make conservation possible in some rich, not-yet-simplified patches of nature (Redford and Mansour 1996). In this spirit, conservationists have revitalized attention to the traditional knowledge of rural people. It seems hopeful that so many indigenous people are not only well-informed about biodiversity, but also willing to share their knowledge with conservationists. Yet obstructions abound.

1980年代晚期，拯救亚马孙森林的国际运动蓬勃发展，激发了一种新的政治形式：原住民领袖与环保人士之间的协作。原住民权利与保护倡议纠缠在一起。这类协作部分受到研究者的启发，他们发现原住民欣赏并管理着与其共处的生物多样性（e.g., Posey 1985）。科学家、行动者和原住民之间在文化上敏感的联盟，似乎有可能在世界上一些富饶且尚未被简化的自然地块中实现保护（Redford and Mansour 1996）。本着这种精神，保护主义者重新关注乡村人的传统知识。如此多原住民不仅熟知生物多样性，而且愿意与保护主义者分享知识，这似乎令人充满希望。然而，阻碍比比皆是。

Political ecologist Søren Hvalkof learns why the Siona Indians of the Ecuadorian Amazon refuse resource extraction contracts: “In impassioned voices they told revolting stories about how [during the early twentieth-century rubber boom] the local rubber patrons and their contractors had murdered, tortured, and abused their folks” (Hvalkof 2000: 87).
政治生态学家索伦·瓦尔科夫（Søren Hvalkof）了解到，厄瓜多尔亚马孙地区的西奥纳印第安人为何拒绝资源开采合同：“他们用激动的声音讲述令人作呕的故事，说〔在20世纪初的橡胶繁荣时期〕当地的橡胶老板及其承包商如何谋杀、折磨和虐待他们的族人”（Hvalkof 2000: 87）。

One obstruction is the terrifying history of past encounters through which indigenous knowledge has entered the metropolitan corpus of science and industry. Most of the economic products in use today for global agriculture and industry were introduced from the knowledges of rural people who knew and used these products; and this process of extraction continues (Juma 1989). This has not been a pretty history of mutual benefit. Infused with practices of enslavement, terror, theft, murder, and deceit, the expansion of European and “international” knowledge of economic products has been deeply entangled with subjugation. The current course of global capitalism suggests that such coercive and unequal collaborations will continue. Many of the most conspicuous models of conservationist collaboration (such as “rainforest marketing,” in which local identification of economic plants is coupled with corporate production and distribution, and “biodiversity prospecting,” in which rural people help scientists gather plants for corporate pharmaceutical development) have suffered from their refusal to repudiate this past history, instead drawing from its legacy of exploitation (Dove 1993; Shiva 1997).

一种阻碍是过去遭遇的可怕历史：原住民的知识正是通过这些遭遇进入科学与工业的大都会知识库。今天用于全球农业和工业的大多数经济产品，都来自那些认识并使用这些产品的乡村人的知识；而这种榨取过程仍在继续（Juma 1989）。这并非一部美好的互利史。欧洲及“国际”关于经济产品的知识扩张，浸透着奴役、恐怖、盗窃、谋杀和欺骗的实践，与征服深深纠缠在一起。全球资本主义当前的进程表明，这类强制性的不平等协作将会继续。许多最显眼的保护主义协作模式——例如“雨林营销”，把当地人对经济植物的鉴定与公司生产和分配结合起来；以及“生物多样性勘探”，由乡村人帮助科学家采集植物，供公司药物开发——都因拒绝摒弃这段历史而受损，反而从剥削的遗产中汲取资源（Dove 1993; Shiva 1997）。

Feminist theorist Noel Sturgeon offers a generous reading of the quirks and promises of U.S. ecofeminism, yet she worries that ecofeminist attention to indigenous knowledge, despite good intentions, reconstitutes white privilege: “One way this occurs is through the racial essentialism of the idea of the indigenous, which erases all difference between and within the categories ‘Native American’ and ‘Third World’ and constitutes them as racialized Others to a white Self that is Western, modern, and industrialized” (Sturgeon 1997: 113).

女性主义理论家诺埃尔·斯特金（Noel Sturgeon）对美国生态女性主义的怪癖与承诺作了宽容的解读，但她担心，生态女性主义对原住民知识的关注，尽管出于善意，却重新构成了白人特权：“这种情况发生的一种方式，是通过‘原住民’观念中的种族本质主义，它抹除了‘美洲原住民’与‘第三世界’这两个类别之间及其内部的全部差异，并把它们建构为一个西方、现代、工业化的白人自我的种族化他者”（Sturgeon 1997: 113）。

Another obstruction is the metropolitan romance that produces the categories with which we know “indigenous” people and “wild” nature. These are modernist categories in negation; they index people and places not included in “modern” landscapes, that is, landscapes in which planners have worked hard to subjugate variety for the cause of regularity, hygiene, property, efficiency, and profit. Because indigenous people and wild nature only exist in opposition to these modernist programs, any generalizations we make about them are likely to be wrong. We quickly ascend to a world of fantasy every time we imagine tribal survival or spirituality, or wild nature’s competitive struggle or harmonious stability. These categories have a limited usefulness in helping us understand the idiosyncratic histories of particular social and natural landscapes. Yet it seems to me that we cannot give up these fantastical categories. It is only because of the protest embedded in them that some conservationists even imagine collaboration across cultures to preserve the variety of nature. The alternative fantasy—a falsely uniform modernism—is much worse.

另一种阻碍是大都会浪漫想象，它生产了我们借以认识“原住民”和“野性”自然的范畴。这些是以否定方式构造的现代主义范畴；它们标示出未被纳入“现代”地景的人民和地点——所谓现代地景，就是规划者为了规整、卫生、财产、效率和利润而竭力征服多样性的地景。由于原住民与野性自然只在与这些现代主义方案对立时才存在，我们对它们作出的任何概括都可能是错的。每当我们想象部落生存或灵性，想象野性自然的竞争斗争或和谐稳定，我们便迅速升入一个幻想世界。这些范畴在帮助我们理解特定社会与自然地景的独特历史方面，作用有限。然而在我看来，我们无法放弃这些幻想性的范畴。正是因为其中嵌入了抗议，一些保护主义者才会想象跨文化协作以保存自然的多样性。另一种幻想——虚假均质的现代主义——要糟糕得多。

Even the staunchly scientific International Union for the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources has suggested that wilderness protection requires working with indigenous peoples: “It is becoming obvious that the key to protecting a cherished landscape lies within the communities that call it home” (Holdgate 1993: v).
就连坚定奉行科学立场的国际自然与自然资源保护联盟也提出，荒野保护需要与原住民合作：“越来越明显的是，保护一片备受珍视的地景的关键，掌握在把它称为家园的社群手中”（Holdgate 1993: v）。

While this argument can lead to oversimplifications, we do not need to reify either indigenous people or wild nature to explore its practical possibilities (Stevens 1997). The crux of the argument about indigenous people and conservation is that the regularizing modern imagination has had such a destructive effect on species diversity that almost any other human lifeway is likely to be better at maintaining it (Banuri and Marglin 1993). Farmers invade tropical forests when they are incorporated into modern political economies (Lohmann 1993). This attention to the historical and cultural specificity of modernist destruction is an important—and promising—divergence from more popular conservationist models, which posit all humanity in conflict with nature. It is worth attending to indigenous-conservationist collaborations just to give them some breathing room.

尽管这一论证可能导致过度简化，我们不必把原住民或野性自然物化，才能探究其实际可能性（Stevens 1997）。关于原住民与保护的论证要点是：规范化的现代想象对物种多样性造成了如此破坏性的影响，以至于几乎任何其他人类生活方式都可能更善于维持多样性（Banuri and Marglin 1993）。农民是在被纳入现代政治经济之后，才侵入热带森林的（Lohmann 1993）。对现代主义破坏的历史与文化特殊性的这种关注，是对更流行的保护主义模式——那些把所有人类都设定为与自然冲突的模式——的一种重要而有希望的偏离。仅仅为了给原住民—保护主义协作一些喘息空间，也值得关注它们。

At a 1998 conference in Georgia, activists and scholars argued about community-based conservation. Both sides agreed that these are some of the most promising conservation programs we know. Yet the scholars insisted, “Aren’t we oversimplifying ‘community’ and ‘nature’?” (Brosius, Tsing, and Zerner 1998).
1998年在佐治亚州的一次会议上，行动者与学者围绕基于社群的保护展开争论。双方都同意，这类保护是我们所知最有希望的保护项目之一。但学者们坚持问道：“我们是不是把‘社群’和‘自然’过度简化了？”（Brosius, Tsing, and Zerner 1998）。

Many critical scholars have given up on conservationists’ interest in indigenous people, categorizing it only as a repetition of metropolitan fantasies and imperial histories. Anthropologists make fun of activists’ stereotypes about other cultures; literary critics trace these stereotypes back through a literary legacy (Ellen 1986; Slater 1995). Political ecologists show the disciplines conservationists impose on rural people and connect these to the history of colonialism (Li 2003b; Neumann 1998). These are crucial critical perspectives. Yet, taken together, they offer a historical metanarrative of imperial modernization in which nothing can happen—good or bad—but more of the same. Familiar heroes and villains are again arrayed on the same battlefield. It is difficult to see how new actors and arguments might ever emerge.

许多批判学者已不再相信保护主义者对原住民的兴趣，只把它归为对大都会幻想和帝国历史的重复。人类学家嘲弄行动者对其他文化的刻板印象；文学批评家把这些刻板印象追溯为一种文学遗产（Ellen 1986; Slater 1995）。政治生态学家揭示保护主义者强加给乡村人的规训，并将其与殖民主义历史联系起来（Li 2003b; Neumann 1998）。这些都是至关重要的批判视角。然而，合在一起，它们提供了一种关于帝国现代化的历史元叙事：在其中，无论好坏，都不可能发生任何事，只会是同一回事的重复。熟悉的英雄与恶人再次列阵于同一战场。很难看出新的行动者和论点如何可能出现。

Scholars have consolidated their critical perspective on conservation by looking for contests in which parties with different stakes—European hunters and African herders, resident farmers and urban nature lovers, foreign activists and native tribes—struggle over the definition and use of nature (Brosius 1999a). This work usefully brings culture and politics together in understanding environmental conflicts; but there are other ways, too, to look at politics and culture. Much less attention has been paid to collaborative relationships through which environmental campaigns have been mounted. Collaboration is not necessarily good for all parties; to study it is not to pretend that easy solutions abound. Collaboration does, however, draw attention to the formation of new cultural and political configurations that change the arena of conflict, rather than just repeating old contests.

学者们通过考察不同利益方——欧洲猎人与非洲牧民、当地农民与城市自然爱好者、外国行动者与原住民部落——围绕自然的定义和使用展开的争夺，巩固了他们对保护的批判视角（Brosius 1999a）。这项工作在理解环境冲突时有效地把文化与政治结合起来；但观察政治与文化还有其他方式。人们对环保运动得以发动的协作关系关注得少得多。协作并不必然对各方都有利；研究它并不等于假装轻易的解决办法比比皆是。然而，协作确实让我们关注新的文化与政治格局的形成，这些格局改变冲突的舞台，而不只是重复旧的争夺。
“Turtles and Teamsters”: The unlikely—and tentative—alliance between labor and environmentalism successfully closed down the World Trade Organization’s meeting in Seattle in 1999 (Berry 1999).
“海龟与卡车司机”：劳工与环保主义之间那个不太可能、且试探性的联盟，成功地使世界贸易组织1999年在西雅图的会议停摆（Berry 1999）。

In this spirit, I stride cautiously but with determination into the arena of conservationist-indigenous alliances. Even as seemingly innocent an activity as making species lists can find itself enmired in condescension and theft: Does the list stereotype indigenous knowledge, limiting future economic and political strategies for the group? Does it erase nascent intellectual property rights or make information available for corporate exploitation? To care about these questions does not turn me away from multicultural environmentalism. Instead, such questions sharpen my attention to the process of collaboration.
本着这种精神，我谨慎而坚定地步入保护主义者—原住民联盟的竞技场。即便像编制物种名录这样看似无害的活动，也可能陷入居高临下与盗窃：名录是否把原住民知识刻板化，从而限制该群体未来的经济和政治策略？它是否抹去初生的知识产权，或让信息可供企业剥削？关心这些问题并不会让我远离多元文化环保主义。相反，这些问题使我对协作过程更加关注。

In drawing attention to our collaborative process, my first two steps are an acknowledgment of eclectic knowledges and overlapping pleasures. List-making is eclectic to the extent that it draws on multiple, fragmentary sources. Furthermore, any list made by two or more people is a negotiated, eclectic product. To acknowledge this eclecticism allows us to admire its creative use of limited materials, rather than to grasp only for scope. It allows us to imagine the list within historically changing conversations, rather than as transcendent knowledge. My input in the species list I made with Uma Adang blended a variety of historically particular genre conventions and forms of curiosity, ranging from scholarly fashions (writing with informants) to activist strategies, from childhood passions (nature appreciation) to fragmented biological observation in Kalimantan and elsewhere. Similarly, Uma Adang brought her own mixture of historically particular goals and resources to the task. The discussion between us sparked new items on the list by juxtaposing and blending our combined intellectual stock within the limited confines of an enthusiastic oral performance, held indoors and in that sometimes awkward mixture of regional dialects with which Uma Adang always directed conversations even without my added blundering.

在把注意力引向我们的协作过程时，我最先采取的两步，是承认兼收并蓄的知识与相互重叠的乐趣。编制名录之所以兼收并蓄，是因为它汲取多个碎片化的来源。此外，任何由两个或更多人共同制作的名录，都是协商出来的杂糅产物。承认这种兼收并蓄，使我们能够欣赏它对有限材料的创造性运用，而不只是追求范围。它让我们把名录想象为处于历史变化的对话之中，而不是超越历史的知识。在与乌玛·阿当共同编制的物种名录中，我的投入混合了多种历史上特定的体裁惯例与好奇形式，从学术风尚（与报道人一起写作）到行动策略，从童年热情（自然欣赏）到在加里曼丹及其他地方碎片化的生物学观察。同样，乌玛·阿当也把她那套历史上特定的目标与资源混合物带入这项工作。我们之间的讨论在一种热情口头表演的有限范围内，通过并置和混合我们合在一起的知识储备，激发出名录上的新条目；这场表演在室内进行，夹杂着乌玛·阿当即使没有我笨拙插嘴也总用来主导谈话的那种有时颇为别扭的地区方言混合。

The eclecticism we produced is perhaps obvious—and I’ve tried to make it visible in the translations I offer by including Latin names only occasionally and by identifying organisms through an irregular mixture of Uma Adang’s and my own commentary. I ignore questions of classification, offering only the negotiated list. I am more interested in introducing my readers to plants and animals than in adding them to a biological or cultural master list. To speak to a heterogeneous readership, I mention, for example, that lalamas (#45) is an aroid, like taro, for those who care; for those who don’t, I hope that the image of heart-shaped leaves by the side of the stream beckons at least a little. This is, then, a motivated set of translations and not a simple addition to either universal or local cultural knowledge.
我们制造出的兼收并蓄也许显而易见——我试着在提供的翻译中让它可见：只偶尔加入拉丁名，并通过乌玛·阿当与我自己的评论不规则混合来辨识生物。我忽略分类问题，只提供协商出来的名录。比起把植物和动物加入某个生物学或文化总表，我更想让读者认识它们。为了面向异质读者，我举例说
（第45条）是一种天南星科植物，像芋头——这话是说给关心的人；对于不关心的人，我希望溪边心形叶子的形象至少能有一点吸引力。因此，这是一组有动机的翻译，而不是对普遍知识或本地文化知识的简单补充。

In other collaborative species lists, the Linnaean Latin name of an organism is paired dichotomously with a “local” name; the Latin name offers international information, while the local name grounds it in a particular place and discovery process. Conservationist-indigenous collaborations have sometimes used these lists to argue that local names on the list represent a codified traditional knowledge, which can match at least in form its scientific counterpart. There are lots of good reasons to codify knowledge. Sometimes such codifications are a tool for historically marginalized people to gain a place in negotiations of their resource rights. Anthropological investigations of the breadth and detail of indigenous knowledge can play an important role in facilitating this process, and I am full of appreciation for such work. However, for the specific task of understanding collaboration, it is necessary to draw attention to the context in which communication and codification occur. This requires acknowledgment of the inevitable eclecticism and serendipity of the knowledge-making process. The systematic study of “Meratus ethnobiology” is another task.

在其他协作性物种名录中，生物的拉丁林奈名与一个“本地”名二元配对；拉丁名提供国际信息，本地名则把它锚定在特定地点和发现过程中。保护主义者与原住民的协作有时利用这类名录论证：名录上的本地名代表一种被编纂成文的传统知识，至少形式上可与科学对应物相匹配。编纂知识有许多好理由。有时这种编纂是历史上被边缘化的人在其资源权谈判中获得位置的工具。对原住民知识之广度与细节的人类学调查，可以在推动这一过程中发挥重要作用，我对此类工作十分赞赏。然而，就理解协作这一特定任务而言，有必要关注传播与编纂发生的语境。这要求承认知识制造过程不可避免的兼收并蓄与机缘。对“梅拉图斯民族生物学”的系统研究是另一项任务。

A concern with collaboration also draws my attention to the overlapping pleasures of list-making. If lists have anything to do with conservation, it is because they exude a certain charisma: They make people exclaim in wonder at the diversity of nature; they can inspire us to preserve that diversity. Yet for urbanites outside of the practices of nature appreciation and conservation biology, such lists often seem dead bureaucratic forms. Who cares whether there are ten species of snails or ten thousand? To ask how list-making works as a form of collaboration in nature appreciation is to make that appreciation palpable. What pleasures motivate each side of the collaboration to participate?
对协作的关注也让我注意到编制名录那些相互重叠的乐趣。如果名录与保护有任何关系，那是因为它们散发出某种感召力：它们让人惊叹自然的多样性；它们能启发我们保护那种多样性。然而，对于自然欣赏和保护生物学实践之外的城市人，这类名录往往显得像僵死的官僚表格。谁在乎蜗牛有十种还是一万种？追问编制名录如何作为一种自然欣赏中的协作形式发挥作用，就是让这种欣赏变得可感。是什么乐趣驱动协作的每一方参与其中？

For Uma Adang, the pleasures have been many. Consider the pleasure of storytelling: It is impossible to tell or listen to stories in Kalimantan without saying the names of plants and animals. People encounter a large variety of plants and animals every day. It is hard to talk about what people are doing or where they have been without talking about plants and animals. One of the pleasures of Uma Adang’s list was its incitement to remember and tell stories.
对乌玛·阿当来说，乐趣有很多。想想讲故事的乐趣：在加里曼丹，讲故事或听故事，不可能不提到植物和动物的名字。人们每天遇到种类繁多的植物和动物。要谈论人们在做什么或去过哪里，很难不谈到植物和动物。乌玛·阿当这份名录的乐趣之一，就是它促使人回忆并讲述故事。

In Kalimantan as in other places, to talk of snakes often provokes stories. When we arrived at snakes in our list, the house began to jump with stories of snake encounters. Uma Adang’s sister told me about the time she was bitten by an ular ambularas. She wasn’t content with a casual tale. In her own intimate mockery of Uma Adang’s oratorical style, which had been so successful in grabbing my attention, she fashioned her story with an air of officious spiritualism: “The snake was coiled around a tree, and when I passed, zap, it bit me in the calf. Another person might have died. But I had an ‘anti’—to drink a tea of the roots of tandoi dug at noon on a Friday. The poison spread up to my head, climbing like a snake’s scales, turning my body cold. It was freezing my flesh. It rose three times and fell again three times. I looked up and saw the rays of the sun spreading like a hand, and I knew I would recover.”
在加里曼丹，和其他地方一样，谈到蛇往往会引出故事。当名录进行到蛇时，屋里开始因遇见蛇的故事而雀跃。乌玛·阿当的姐妹给我讲了她被
咬伤的那一次。她不满足于随便讲讲。她以自己那种亲密的方式嘲弄乌玛·阿当曾成功吸引我注意的演讲风格，带着一种一本正经的灵性气派讲述故事：“那条蛇盘在树上，我经过时，嗖的一声，它咬了我的小腿。换个人可能就死了。但我有‘解药’（
根泡的茶。毒往上爬到我的头，像蛇鳞一样攀爬，让我的身体发冷。它冻住我的肉。它升起来三次，又落下三次。我抬头看见阳光像一只手一样铺开，我就知道我会好起来。”

Immersed in stories of snakes, I couldn’t hold back my own story of an encounter with a king cobra outside a village in the mountains. I was standing by the river when the great dark snake came speeding out of the bushes following a frog. With a heroic leap, the frog jumped into the water. The snake stopped at the shore, by now only a few feet away from me. It was standing with its head at least four feet off the ground. We turned toward each other and gave each other a long, long look. Panicking, I turned and took two steps before realizing the impossibility of flight across the tumbled riverside boulders. I turned back. The snake was gone. Shaken, I returned to the house. “That was no ordinary snake,” said my host. “If you had stayed, it would have spoken to you and given you a magical gift.” Back in the United States, I came across the king cobra’s picture in a book on snakes in the library, and it was only then that I found that the snakes I had come to know as tadung were also cobras.

沉浸在蛇的故事中，我也忍不住讲起自己在山里一个村外遇见眼镜王蛇的经历。我站在河边，那条巨大的黑蛇追着一只青蛙，从灌木丛中疾驰而出。青蛙英勇地一跃，跳进水里。蛇停在岸边，离我只有几英尺远。它立起身子，头至少离地四英尺。我们转向彼此，久久地对视。我惊慌失措，转身走了两步，才意识到要越过河边七零八落的巨石逃跑是不可能的。我转回身。蛇不见了。我惊魂未定地回到屋里。“那可不是普通的蛇，”我的主人说，“如果你留下来，它会跟你说话，给你一件神奇的礼物。”回到美国后，我在图书馆一本讲蛇的书里看到眼镜王蛇的图片，直到那时才发现，我逐渐认识为

The stories we exchanged about snakes focused on the unusual and the unexpected. But the pleasures of the everyday and the ordinary are also told in stories and even lists of diversity. Plants and animals figure everywhere in Meratus Dayak livelihood practices and the stories through which they are savored and shared. Discussion of cultivation and gathering, for example, is all about the diversity of plants and animals and tastes and habitats. Foods are diverse in both forests and fields: the range of food plants gathered from the forest is matched by the range of crop varieties nurtured in swidden fields. Swidden plant variety is mulled over and discussed every time something is to be planted; every time a neighbor comes to ask for one of those ripe squash; every time a young couple borrows not just one but many kinds of rice seed to extend their social networks; every time a child demands that variety of banana and not that other one.

我们交换的蛇故事集中在不寻常和出乎意料的事上。但日常与平凡的乐趣，也通过故事，甚至通过多样性名录讲述。在梅拉图斯达雅克人的生计实践以及他们借以品味和分享这些实践的故事中，植物和动物无处不在。例如，关于耕种与采集的讨论，全都是植物、动物、味道和生境的多样性。森林和田野里的食物都多样：从森林采集的食物植物范围，与刀耕火种田里培育的作物品种范围相配。每当要种下什么东西，每当邻居来讨要一个熟南瓜，每当一对年轻夫妇为了扩展社会网络而借来不止一种、而是许多种稻种，每当一个孩子要求那种香蕉而不是另一种，刀耕火种田里的植物多样性就会被反复思量、讨论。

For an observer used to imagining agriculture as cleanly weeded lines of corn, wheat, or tomatoes, but not all tossed together, the most amazing thing about a Meratus swidden field is the extraordinary number of plants growing together in the same small spot. There may be trees saved from the forest that was cut to make the field: fruit trees, honey trees, sugar palms. Fallen trunks and stumps, sometimes resprouting, litter the ground. Between them grow an exuberance of plants: not only grains, such as rice, corn, millet, and job’s tears, but root crops, such as taro, cassava, and sweet potatoes, as well as beans crawling up the stumps, eggplant bushes five feet high, dense clumps of sugar cane, spreading squashes, gangling banana and papaya trees, gingers and basils and medicinal plants, and on and on. The field is a scene of enormous variety, and it would be a mistake to ignore this variety in thinking about the appreciation of biodiversity, although, of course, most (but not all) of this variety represents cultivated variety and not wild nature. A sharp line between nature and agriculture will not help here: To appreciate Meratus Dayak pleasures in biodiversity, the swidden field is an important site. And while this variety is well known to connoisseurs of shifting cultivation (Conklin 1975), it is worth giving other readers a quick look at a field.

对于一个习惯把农业想象成整齐除草的行列——玉米、小麦或番茄的行列，而非全都混在一起——的观察者来说，梅拉图斯刀耕火种田最惊人之处，是在同一小块土地上一起生长的植物种类之多。那里可能有从为开田而砍伐的森林中保留下来的树：果树、蜜树、糖棕。倒下的树干和树桩散落在地上，有时还会重新发芽。它们之间蓬勃生长着各种植物：不仅有谷物，如稻、玉米、小米和薏苡，还有根茎类作物，如芋头、木薯和甘薯，以及攀上树桩的豆子、五英尺高的茄丛、茂密的甘蔗、蔓延的南瓜、瘦长的香蕉和木瓜树、姜、罗勒和药用植物，等等。田地是一幅巨大多样性的景象；在思考生物多样性欣赏时忽视这种多样性将是个错误，尽管当然，这种多样性的大部分（并非全部）代表栽培品种，而非野性自然。自然与农业之间的鲜明界线在这里无济于事：要欣赏梅拉图斯达雅克人的生物多样性乐趣，刀耕火种田是一个重要场所。虽然这种多样性对刀耕火种的行家来说众所周知（Conklin 1975），仍值得让其他读者也快速看一眼田地。

The production of rice is the centerpiece of the Meratus swidden field: It frames the schedule for labor and forms the standard for sufficiency. Most people who make a field grow between three and thirty varieties of rice. Uma Adang and I decided not to list rice varieties because of my mistaken recollection that we had done so on an earlier occasion; I’m sure they would have added many entries to our list. But the luxuriance of rice varieties is more than matched in the diversity of vegetables grown together with rice, and here Uma Adang listed with exuberance.
稻米生产是梅拉图斯刀耕火种田的核心：它框定了劳作日程，并构成充足的标准。大多数开田的人种植三到三十个稻米品种。乌玛·阿当和我决定不列出稻米品种，因为我错误地记得我们早先已经列过；我确信，这些品种本会给名录增添许多条目。然而，与稻米一起种植的蔬菜，其多样性甚至超过稻米品种的丰富程度，而乌玛·阿当在列这些蔬菜时兴致勃勃。

Variety is at one level a matter of taste. Who would grow only one variety of bananas (and certainly not the bland and pasty giants of North American grocery stores) when more than thirty varieties beckon? Red, long, fruity bananas, or tiny, delicate yellow bananas, or bright orange, saucer-like bananas, or hard, astringent roasting bananas, or even wild bananas, sweet, but full of seeds: In these, a person can choose and vary snacks. Food habits sometimes follow health precautions: nursing mothers, for example, are careful about the varieties of beans and cucumbers they eat, lest residues passed in breast milk irritate their babies. Tastes also expand to respond to the demands of the market when vegetables are grown as cash crops. Chili peppers are a women’s cash crop, picked pepper by pepper in the hot sun, but easy to ask the market-bound men to transport and not so valuable that the men are tempted to take the small gains. The tiniest varieties—which take so long to pick—are the most valuable; the longer ones take less time and bring a lesser price. Most women mix plantings and move back and forth in harvesting. Besides, some years, one variety thrives while the others wilt. Some rice varieties are more sensitive to pest damage than others. And when one rice variety after another succumbs to drought, there are hardy cassava roots and long-growing taro roots from last year and quick-growing millet at the edge of the field—not to mention plants from the forest.

品种在某种意义上关乎口味。当三十多个品种在招手时，谁会只种一种香蕉（当然不会是北美杂货店里那种淡而无味、糊状的巨型香蕉）？红色、细长、果味浓郁的香蕉，或娇小精致的黄色香蕉，或鲜橙色、碟状的香蕉，或坚硬涩口的烤香蕉，甚至野生香蕉，甜却满是种子：人们可以在这些之中选择，让零食富于变化。饮食习惯有时遵循健康预防措施：例如，哺乳的母亲会小心选择吃哪些豆子和黄瓜，以免通过母乳传出的残余物刺激婴儿。当蔬菜作为经济作物种植时，口味也会扩展以回应市场需求。辣椒是女性的经济作物，在烈日下一个一个地采摘，但容易请去市场的男人运输，又不那么值钱，男人们不会受诱惑拿走这点小收益。最小的品种——采摘耗时最长——最有价值；较长的品种耗时较少，卖价也较低。大多数妇女混合种植，并在收获时轮流采摘不同品种。此外，有些年份，一个品种茁壮，其他品种却枯萎。有些稻米品种比其他品种更易受虫害。当一种又一种稻米品种在干旱中败下阵来，还有耐旱的木薯根、去年留下的生长期长的芋头根，以及田边快速生长的小米——更不用说森林里的植物了。

Variety responds to and expands the ecological niches of the swidden field. Crops cycle, reusing the same space. Corn is sometimes planted in the still-warm ashes of a newly burnt swidden field, with rice planted later between the growing cornstalks. The corn will be harvested before the rice flowers. Banana plants take eighteen months to bear fruit; sugar cane takes more than a year to reach an edible size; papaya trees, when they finally fruit, bear for at least five years. All of these are planted early in the making of a swidden, with the expectation that they will be fruitful only while a second crop of rice grows, and perhaps long after as the swidden slowly grows back into forest. Thus, too, rattans and trees— coffee, rubber, fruits, sugar palms—are planted in the swidden, with the expectation of an even later harvest amidst growing forest plants.

品种回应并扩展刀耕火种田的生态位。作物轮换，重复使用同一空间。玉米有时种在新烧田里仍有余温的灰烬中，之后在生长的玉米秆之间种稻。玉米会在稻开花前收获。香蕉要十八个月才结果；甘蔗要一年多才长到可食的大小；木瓜树终于结果时，至少连续结果五年。所有这些都在开田初期种下，预期它们要到第二茬稻生长时才开始产出，或许在田慢慢长回森林之后很久仍会结果。棕榈藤和树——咖啡、橡胶、果树、糖棕——也以同样方式种在田里，预期在日益增长的森林植物之间更晚收获。

Spatial niches are created as well as niches in time. Beans are planted around a stump to give the vines support. Job’s tears form a line of demarcation where two fields meet. Almost any vegetable responds well to being planted in the ash heaps that result from the secondary burning of piled debris; this is a privilege not granted to the rice, the green rows of which blanket the field. Some plants, such as cock’s comb and basil, are grown to add color and fragrance to this blanket. Meanwhile, self-seeding and regrowing forest plants are encouraged to provide more variety to the swidden’s vegetables and medicinal plants.
空间生态位与时间生态位一同被创造出来。豆子种在树桩周围，藤蔓便有了支撑。薏苡在两块田相接处形成分界线。几乎任何蔬菜种在由堆积碎屑二次焚烧形成的灰堆里都长得好；这是水稻没有的特权，稻的绿色行列像毯子一样覆盖田地。有些植物，如鸡冠花和罗勒，被种来为这条毯子增添色彩和香气。同时，自播和再生的森林植物受到鼓励，以为刀耕火种田的蔬菜和药用植物提供更多变化。

For those of us more accustomed to agricultural systems that feature single crops in straight rows, the swidden is a wonderland of variety. How can a farmer keep track of so many kinds of plants, each with its own cycle of production and needs for nurturance? Meditating on this question, I recall that plantation agriculture, the industrialization of farming developed with European expansion, was invented self-consciously to harness coerced, and particularly slave labor. The enslaved or otherwise alienated farm worker will not keep track of variety; it is all overseers can do to make him or her care for one crop. Modern agriculture draws on the plantation heritage to create field systems that do not require nuanced attention from the farmers; field laborers and machinery can usually do the job. Under these conditions, it is difficult to grow more than one crop with one set of requirements. Before we naturalize these conditions as the only way to make plants grow for human uses, we might return to look at swiddens.

对于我们这些更习惯单一行列、单一作物农业系统的人来说，刀耕火种田是一片多样性的奇境。农民如何照看这么多种植物，每一种都有自己的生产周期和培育需求？思考这个问题时，我想起种植园农业——随欧洲扩张发展起来的农业工业化——是自觉地发明出来以利用强制劳动，尤其是奴隶劳动的。被奴役或以其他方式被异化的农业工人不会去照看多样性；监工能做的，只是让他或她关心一种作物。现代农业借助种植园遗产，创造出不需要农民细致关注的田制；田间劳动者和机械通常就能完成工作。在这些条件下，很难用一套需求种植一种以上作物。在我们把这些条件自然化为人类利用植物生长的唯一方式之前，不妨回头看看刀耕火种田。

The variety of swidden vegetables also can remind us of the inextricability of aesthetics and survival. Meratus grow many kinds of crops because they value variety for its taste, for the sociability it allows, for its sheer exuberance, and because it increases the chances of a bountiful harvest. Crop variety guards against crop failure due to pests, climate, or soil conditions. Crop variety invites borrowing and giving of samples, seeds, and cuttings, and it ties farmers to a wide social network, near and far. Crop variety is valued for the beauty it gives the field and as a sign of the prowess of the farmer. The interweaving of aesthetics and survival here reminds us not to consider the Meratus a “spiritual” people who love nature only for its cosmic beauty, without the materialist priorities of modern urban life. It reminds us not to consider the Meratus a “hungry” people who think only of hand-to-mouth survival and, unlike modern urbanites, value nature only to the extent it can feed them. These are the two most common stereotypes not only of “tribes” but of rural people in general. Yet the modernist dichotomy that drives each, in which aesthetics is either higher or lower but certainly separate from survival, is of no use in describing commitments to biodiversity most anywhere in the world, and certainly not in Kalimantan. Each time we begin to be seduced by slogans such as “nature appreciation is an idea only in the privileged West,” or “Third World people care about development not species conservation,” or “religion X is a form of conservation,” we might want to remember the variety of vegetables in the Meratus swidden field.

刀耕火种蔬菜的多样性也提醒我们，审美与生存不可分割。梅拉图斯人种植多种作物，是因为他们珍视品种带来的味道、它促成的社交性、它纯粹的繁茂，也因为它增加丰收的机会。作物多样性可防范虫害、气候或土壤条件造成的歉收。作物多样性促成样本、种子和插条的借出与赠送，把农民联结进远近广阔的社会网络。作物多样性因它赋予田地的美、作为农民本领的标志而受到珍视。这里审美与生存的交织提醒我们，不要把梅拉图斯人看作只为宇宙之美而爱自然的“灵性”民族，没有现代城市生活的物质主义优先事项。它也提醒我们，不要把梅拉图斯人看作只想着糊口生存的“饥饿”民族，与现代城市人不同，只在自然能喂饱他们时才重视自然。这不仅是对“部落”，也是对一般乡村人最常见的两种刻板印象。然而，驱动这两种刻板印象的现代主义二分——审美要么更高，要么更低，但肯定与生存分离——对于描述世界上大多数地方对生物多样性的承诺毫无用处，在加里曼丹尤其如此。每当我们开始被“自然欣赏只是特权西方的观念”“第三世界人民关心发展，不关心物种保护”或“宗教X是一种保护形式”之类的口号所诱惑，也许都该想想梅拉图斯刀耕火种田里的蔬菜多样性。

But we were speaking of pleasures, and particularly the pleasures of listing species, and I have not yet mentioned the most obvious: the making of the list itself. Uma Adang loved the idea that I was writing down the list and enumerating each item. For ease of taking notes, I started my numeration with “one” every time we switched to a new life-form. But Uma Adang always wanted to know the total, and I added and added again each time we took a break. Making it past one thousand items became a goal. The list took on all the pleasures of writing, counting, and classifying: Uma Adang and I were pretending to be bureaucrats with the authority of state and international codification. We were ordering the world by naming it. As Uma Adang explained to me, “Everyone knows these names; but not everyone knows how to organize them properly.” True enough; these names were common knowledge, but few of my Meratus friends would have had Uma Adang’s memory, patience, and fun in making the list.

但我们谈的是乐趣，尤其是为物种编列名录的乐趣，而我还没有提到最明显的一种：名录本身的制作。乌玛·阿当喜欢我在写下名录、逐项编号这一想法。为了方便记录，每当换到一个新的生物类别，我就从“一”重新开始编号。但乌玛·阿当总想知道总数，于是每次休息时，我一次次往上加。让总数超过一千项成了一个目标。名录承接了书写、计数和分类的全部乐趣：乌玛·阿当和我假装自己是拥有国家及国际编纂权威的官僚。我们通过命名来安排世界。正如乌玛·阿当向我解释的：“人人都知道这些名字；但不是人人都知道如何把它们恰当地组织起来。”确实如此；这些名字是常识，但我的梅拉图斯朋友中很少有人有乌玛·阿当那样的记忆力、耐心和编名录的乐趣。

Consider mushrooms. With fungi (unlike snakes), I might have recognized at least cosmopolitan families and species if we had identified them in the field—or talked about them in detail. But Uma Adang was so enthralled with list-making at that point that she sped through, hardly minding my questions, building the list. We did pretty well, for a memory project. But I hadn’t known most of these names, and I was barely able to get her to offer me the briefest of descriptions: whether the fungus grew on wood or on the ground; whether it was edible or inedible. The lure of adding new items was too great to be patient with questions.
想想菌类。如果是真菌（不像蛇），如果我们在野外辨识或详细谈论过它们，我或许至少能认出一些广泛分布的科和种。但乌玛·阿当那时太着迷于编名录，飞快地往下走，几乎不在意我的问题，只顾着构建名录。作为一个凭记忆完成的项目，我们做得相当不错。但其中大多数名字我都不认识，我好不容易才让她给出最短的描述：真菌长在木头上还是地上；可食还是不可食。增添新条目的诱惑太大，容不得耐心回答问题。

Uma Adang is not alone among Meratus Dayaks in liking to make species lists. When I first began research in the area, species lists were one of the first ways I learned to have rich conversations with the people I met. I drew a blank asking abstract questions about gender or power, but I could tell right away that people enjoyed telling me which fish were in the river, which insects made noises, which fruits they hoped to harvest, which trees yielded good firewood. Sometimes I heard children teaching their younger siblings words by having them repeat a list of plants or animals. Uma Adang took this local genre and did her best to use it as a connection to international sources of knowledge. She enjoyed it both as bureaucratic form and as millenial science. She made herself cosmopolitan by making this globalism her own.

在喜欢编制物种名录这一点上，乌玛·阿当在梅拉图斯达雅克人中并不孤单。当我最初在这个地区开始研究时，物种名录是我学会与人进行丰富交谈的最早方式之一。我提出关于性别或权力的抽象问题时，往往得不到回应，但我能立刻看出，人们喜欢告诉我河里有哪种鱼、哪种昆虫发出鸣声、他们希望收获哪些果实、哪些树能提供好柴火。有时我听到孩子让弟弟妹妹重复一份植物或动物名录来教他们词语。乌玛·阿当接过这种本地体裁，尽力把它用作通往国际知识来源的连接。她既把它当作官僚形式，也当作千禧年科学来享受。她通过把这种全球主义变成自己的东西，使自己成为世界主义者。

Sometimes too, the urgency and authority of the list allowed misinterpretations within the eclectic web we wove. The most striking instance occurred when I asked Uma Adang whether rocks have names. I was thinking of a conversation with another Meratus friend who had told me that he differentiated between “living” rocks and “dead” rocks: basalt and sandstone were his respective examples. He thought living rocks could reproduce themselves, although slowly and surreptitiously. Uma Adang mistook my meaning. She began to list the geographical names of the locally prominent karst formations, moving from one end to the other of the area she had demarcated as “local.” I couldn’t stop her no matter how hard I tried; she insisted on finishing. And, although I had a difficult time trying to put it into my list, it was a nice demonstration of the importance of locality in her idea of the globalist project.

有时，名录的紧迫性与权威也使我们编织的兼收并蓄之网内部出现误解。最引人注目的例子发生在我问乌玛·阿当岩石是否有名字的时候。我当时想到与另一位梅拉图斯朋友的谈话，他告诉我，他区分“活的”岩石和“死的”岩石：玄武岩和砂岩分别是他的例子。他认为活岩石能自我繁殖，虽然缓慢而隐蔽。乌玛·阿当误解了我的意思。她开始列举当地显著喀斯特地貌的地理名称，从她划定为“本地”的区域一端列到另一端。无论我怎么努力都阻止不了她；她坚持要列完。尽管我很难把它放进我的名录，这件事很好地表明，在她的全球主义工程观念中，本地性有多么重要。

Despite such reasonably irrelevant fun, there are two reasons I offer this list in the margin of my text. First, it can remind both conservationists and scholars of why we might want to reach out across cultures to understand and advocate the pleasures of biodiversity. Cultural theorists need to know that the variety of nature is an important rural concern, not just an imposition of metropolitan scientists. Conservationists need to know that our knowledge of nature is always cultural knowledge, whether we are scientists or farmers. To be aware of the necessity for careful coalitions with those whose knowledge and pleasure comes from other sources is the beginning of a nonimperialist environmentalism.

尽管有这些相当无关紧要的乐趣，我仍把这份名录放在正文边缘，有两个理由。第一，它可以提醒保护主义者和学者，我们为什么可能想要跨越文化去理解并倡导生物多样性的乐趣。文化理论家需要知道，自然的多样性是乡村人的一项重要关切，而不只是大都会科学家强加的东西。保护主义者需要知道，我们对自然的认识始终是文化知识，无论我们是科学家还是农民。意识到有必要与那些知识和乐趣来自其他来源的人建立谨慎联盟，是走向非帝国主义环保主义的开端。

Second, Uma Adang’s list offers a vivid image of global friction. The list is self-consciously globalist: an entry into a world-making millenial project. It is self-consciously localized: following the contours of local geographies and their plant and animal residents. It is self-consciously culturally particular and cross-culturally generative: it speaks of the possibility of multiple kinds of translation. The list offers the pleasure of making a widely circulating form come to life in the terrain around one’s home place, and for foreigners as well as local folks. The list builds a situated “point of view” from which to engage globalism. The ability to work from a point of view is the very thing scholars need to assess scale-making claims and practices.

第二，乌玛·阿当的名录提供了全球摩擦的生动形象。这份名录自觉地是全球主义的：它进入一个创造世界的千禧年工程。它自觉地本地化：顺着本地地理及其动植物居民的轮廓展开。它自觉地在文化上特殊，又跨文化地生成：它言说多种翻译的可能性。名录带来的乐趣，是让一种广泛流通的形式在家乡周边的土地上活起来，对本地人和外国人都是如此。名录建立起一个“有位置的观点”，借以介入全球主义。能够从一种观点出发工作，正是学者评估尺度制造主张与实践所需要的。
But how can I end without a celebration of fungal abundance?
但是，不赞美一下真菌的丰盛，我如何能结束呢？
